title: Dual-Kernel Adapter: Expanding Spatial Horizons for Data-Constrained Medical Image Analysis
one_liner: When medical labels are scarce, standard adapters see too little spatial context; this paper adds parallel large and small local filters so the adapter can capture long-range structure without losing fine detail.
lead: Adapters are small trainable modules inserted into a frozen backbone so that only a small part of the network must be updated. In low-data medical imaging, the paper finds that standard adapters can perform worse than linear probing when training data drops below about one percent. Their diagnosis is that the effective receptive field, meaning the part of the image that strongly influences one output unit, shrinks too much under scarce supervision. The proposed Dual-Kernel Adapter, where kernel means a wide local filter, reduces features, reshapes them back to the image grid, applies one large branch and one small depthwise filter in parallel, sums the two outputs, and projects back up with a residual connection. The large branch carries broad anatomical context, while the small branch keeps local lesion detail.

problem.h2: Why standard adapters break under extreme data scarcity
paras: Compact tuning, meaning updating only a small trainable part of the network, is attractive in medical imaging because labels are expensive and the backbone is already pretrained. But a small trainable module is only useful if it can still learn the spatial cues needed by the target task. In medical images, boundaries can be weak, lesions can be tiny, and diagnosis often depends on broad context around a local pattern.

The paper shows that when data are very scarce, a standard adapter does not learn that context well. Even though the backbone is frozen, the adapter still has to decide which spatial evidence matters for the new domain. With too little supervision, its influence stays local and the effective receptive field contracts.

That is why simple linear probing can sometimes beat the adapter. The linear head at least reads stable backbone features directly, while the adapter may inject poorly learned local changes that distort those features.

callout.html: Build an adapter with two parallel depthwise branches, one with a very large local filter and one with a small local filter, so the trainable module has an architectural bias toward both broad context and local detail.

paras: The paper changes the adapter from a mainly channel-mixing bottleneck into a spatial module with built-in long-range and short-range image processing.
object.object: The adapter's effective receptive field under scarce supervision

steps.text: Project the backbone features into a smaller channel space so the adapter stays light.
Reshape patch features back into a two-dimensional grid so spatial filtering can be applied directly.
Apply one large local filter for broad context and one small local filter for nearby detail, with one filter per channel.
Add the branch outputs, pass them through GELU, project back to the original width, and add a residual connection.
Train the adapter and the linear head at different step sizes so the head can adapt quickly without destabilizing the new spatial module.

hidden.name: How much of the image actually influences a prediction
paras: A model can have a large formal field of view and still depend mainly on a small active region. The paper focuses on the effective receptive field, which measures the image area that strongly affects one output location. Under low data, that active area can collapse even when the architecture seems wide enough on paper.

This hidden field matters because many medical decisions depend on dispersed cues. A small lesion can only be interpreted correctly if the model also sees surrounding tissue pattern, shape, and position.

heat.caption: Darker means prediction quality depends more on that factor.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is how much image area the adapter is really using when it decides.
The observed failure of standard adapters in low-data medical imaging is linked to a reduced effective receptive field.

paras: The large branch gives the adapter an architectural path for long-range information even when labels are scarce. That matters because learning broad spatial coupling from scratch is hard with little supervision. A very large depthwise filter already mixes distant locations, so the module does not need many examples to discover that such context should be available.

The small branch prevents the opposite error. If the adapter used only a broad filter, small lesions and thin boundaries could be blurred or dominated by surrounding tissue. The small branch preserves short-range contrast and edge structure, so the fused output can carry both coarse context and fine detail.

The paper also reports that asynchronous learning rates matter. The classifier head and adapter play different roles: the head must quickly align features to labels, while the adapter must slowly learn a new spatial correction. Separate step sizes help because they stop the adapter from moving too aggressively in the earliest low-data updates.

stages.s: Frozen backbone features from a medical image
Down-project and reshape to image grid
Parallel large and small depthwise filters
Fuse branches and add residual path
Better use of context because the adapter can read both broad and local evidence

charts.title: Standard adapter
charts.note: The adapter is acceptable with enough labels, but low-data tuning shrinks the active spatial field, so distant cues are not used when the task needs them.

charts.title: Dual-Kernel Adapter
charts.note: The large branch keeps broad spatial coupling available and the small branch preserves fine detail, so the adapter has a stronger built-in preference for the two kinds of evidence the task needs under scarce supervision because each branch already handles one of those roles before learning begins.

items.b: Large filters can over-smooth rare local cues.
items.html: If the large branch dominates, tiny structures may be diluted by surrounding tissue, especially on tasks where a small abnormality is the main signal.

items.b: Scarce labels can still be too scarce.
items.html: The architecture gives a better bias, but if labels are nearly absent or badly mismatched to the target domain, even the improved adapter may not learn a reliable correction because the supervision still does not tell the module which broad and local cues matter.
The paper's large and small filter sizes work well on its benchmarks, but another imaging scale or resolution may need a different balance between broad context and local detail.
The method is useful when the target task needs both wide anatomical context and fine lesion evidence, because the adapter has an explicit path for both.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a pretrained vision backbone and fine-tune it on a small medical classification or segmentation dataset at several label fractions. Compare linear probing, a standard adapter, a large-only branch, a small-only branch, and the dual-branch design. Plot both task performance and an effective receptive field visualization for each setup.

The demo should let the user switch between data fractions. That matters because the paper's claim is about a failure mode that only becomes clear when supervision is scarce, not when the model has abundant labels.
demo.closing: The demo proves the method if the dual-branch adapter stays ahead of the standard adapter as labels shrink and if its receptive-field map remains visibly broader.

math.words: The module projects features down, applies a large and a small depthwise filter in parallel on the image grid, adds those responses, applies GELU, and projects back up before adding the residual path.
math.equation: DKA(x) = x + Up( GELU( LargeDW( Down(x) ) + SmallDW( Down(x) ) ) )
symbols: input feature map from the frozen backbone
linear down-projection into a smaller channel space
depthwise branch with a large local filter
depthwise branch with a small local filter
linear up-projection back to the original channel width

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose one lesion is small but sits inside a wider tissue pattern.
The small branch responds to the lesion edge and local contrast.
The large branch responds to the surrounding pattern spread over a wider area.
Adding the two responses gives a feature that contains both signals before the head reads it.
If training data are scarce, this built-in split is easier to learn from than asking one generic adapter path to discover both kinds of spatial evidence on its own.

math.note: The equation matters because the two branches are parallel, not sequential, so each branch can preserve its own spatial role before fusion.
